query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) engineered to develop coherent nanoprecipitates (via controlled compositional modification) will show significantly improved ductility compared to its conventional counterpart because the coherent interfaces promote smoother dislocation transmission and reduce stress concentrations.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline tungsten-based refractory HEA that exhibits high strength but limited ductility due to its microstructure lacking engineered coherent nanoprecipitates.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of the alloy composition to induce stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs) during standard processing at ambient conditions.
generation.conditions: Ambient temperature tensile testing following synthesis under standard processing conditions (e.g., arc-melting and appropriate heat treatments) with compositional modifications designed to form SCCP microstructures.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of coherent nanoprecipitates (SCCPs) that create interfaces promoting dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: The coherent interfaces between the matrix and nanoprecipitates facilitate easier dislocation transmission and relieve local stress concentrations, thereby delaying crack initiation and allowing enhanced plastic deformation (i.e., improved ductility).
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified tungsten-based refractory HEA will exhibit an increased tensile ductility (e.g., ductility above 10–15% at ambient temperature), while maintaining high strength.
generation.baseline: The unmodified tungsten-based refractory HEA without SCCPs, which typically shows ultrahigh strength but limited ductility due to stress concentration at unmodified microstructural features.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to be limited to processing conditions that allow formation of the coherent nanoprecipitation structure; deviations in processing (e.g., different temperatures, cooling rates) or compositions outside the studied window may not yield the expected ductility improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The precise compositional thresholds and processing parameters for achieving the optimal balance between nanoprecipitate formation and ductility are not fully determined, and further testing is required to quantify the effect size and determine the robustness of the improvement across different processing scales.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of tungsten-based refractory HEAs: one with the optimized compositional modification aimed at producing coherent nanoprecipitates and one control group with the baseline composition. Both sets will be processed under identical conditions and subjected to standard tensile tests at ambient temperature.
measurements: Tensile elongation (ductility) measurements via tensile testing
Quantitative microstructural characterization (using SEM and EBSD) to confirm the presence and distribution of coherent nanoprecipitates
Measurement of yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in tensile ductility compared to the baseline group, or if microstructural analysis does not confirm the presence of coherent nanoprecipitates correlating with ductility improvements, then the hypothesis that the engineered SCCPs are responsible for the ductility enhancement is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering
